title: The て-form
titleJp: たべて・のんで・いって
canDo: I can make the て-form of any る-verb on the spot: たべる → たべて, あける → あけて.
I can make the て-form of う-verbs from their last syllable, using the table: かう → かって, のむ → のんで, かく → かいて, いそぐ → いそいで, はなす → はなして.
I can avoid the traps: いく → いって (not いいて); かえる and はいる are う-verbs (かえって, はいって).
I can conjugate the irregulars する → して and くる → きて, including compounds (べんきょうして).
I can work out a verb's group from the ます-form I already know.

blocks.t: Warm-up: say out loud the ます-form of 10 verbs you already know (たべます, のみます…)
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each verb and repeat it twice, saying its group (る, う or irregular)
Grammar: the 3 points, reciting the table and saying each example out loud
て-form video (block 6): pause and conjugate before the teacher does
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write down in your notebook the verbs you got wrong

skills: Knowing the ます-form of verbs (たべます, のみます, いきます…) and that there are three groups: る-verbs, う-verbs and irregulars (lesson 03-1).
Reading hiragana fluently: this lesson swaps syllables all the time (む → んで, く → いて), and the small っ makes a difference.
This lesson is only about forming the て-form. Using it starts in lesson 06-2, so don't worry yet about building sentences with it.

vocab.en: to get up, to wake up (る-verb)
to go back, to return home (う-verb, despite the -eru ending)
to play, to have fun, to hang out (う-verb)
to go (う-verb, with an exception in the て-form)

grammar.title: The て-form and る-verbs
grammar.gloss: the connector piece; る → て
grammar.explanation:
The て-form is a **connector piece**. It has no tense (present or past) and cannot end a sentence by itself: it attaches to something else, and that something, at the end of the sentence, decides the meaning. In Genki Lesson 6 it becomes a request (〜てください), a sequence of actions (lesson 06-2), permission (〜てもいいです) and prohibition (〜てはいけません, lesson 06-3). So today the focus is only on **forming** it. Using it comes in the next lessons.
• **It is not a past tense.** It looks a lot like the past short form you'll meet in lesson 09-1 (たべた), but たべて alone never means "ate".
• **る-verbs: drop る and add て.** たべる → たべて · みる → みて · おきる → おきて · あける → あけて · わすれる → わすれて.
• **Why る-verbs are so regular:** a る-verb has one base that never changes (たべ-, み-, あけ-), and every form just replaces る with an ending: たべ-ます, たべ-て, and later たべ-ない, たべ-た. Some guides (Sakubi, for one) call them "one-form" verbs for this reason. う-verbs are "five-form" verbs: their last sound changes from form to form (かく → かきます → かいて), which is why they need the table in point 4b.
• **Shortcut from the ます-form:** with る-verbs, just swap ます for て. たべます → たべて, しめます → しめて.
• **How do you know a verb is a る-verb?** Every る-verb ends in **-iru** or **-eru** (みる, あける). The reverse is not true: かえる and はいる end that way and are う-verbs (point 4b). A verb that does **not** end in -iru/-eru is never a る-verb: it is a う-verb or an irregular.
• **A clue from the ます-form:** if the sound before ます is an **e** sound (たべます, あけます, ねます), the verb is definitely a る-verb. If it is an **i** sound (みます, のみます), it could be either group, and you need to know the dictionary form.
grammar.structure: [る-verb] − る + て   (たべる → たべて)

examples.jp: ごはんを 食べる → ごはんを 食べて
examples.kana: ごはんを たべる → ごはんを たべて
examples.romaji: gohan o taberu → gohan o tabete
examples.en: to eat a meal → て-form (roughly "eat a meal and…")

examples.jp: まどを あける → まどを あけて
examples.kana: まどを あける → まどを あけて
examples.romaji: mado o akeru → mado o akete

examples.jp: テレビを 見る → テレビを 見て
examples.kana: テレビを みる → テレビを みて
examples.romaji: terebi o miru → terebi o mite

pitfalls: Don't stick て onto the whole ます-form: たべますて ✗ → たべて ✓. The shortcut is to SWAP ます for て, and it only works for る-verbs and the two irregulars (point 4c).
With る-verbs the ending is always て, never で: たべて ✓, たべで ✗. で only appears with some う-verbs (4b).
かえる (to go home) and はいる (to enter) look like る-verbs, but they are う-verbs: かえって ✓, はいって ✓. For these two verbs, かえて ✗ and はいて ✗.

The て-form is not a past tense, and on its own it doesn't end a polite sentence: "I watched TV yesterday" is きのう テレビを 見て ✗ → きのう テレビを 見ました ✓. A bare 見て。 sounds like a casual request ("look!"). For now, always complete it: 見てください, 見てもいいです…
howToStudy: Speaking: say these pairs in rhythm, 3 rounds in a row: たべる-たべて, みる-みて, おきる-おきて, ねる-ねて, あける-あけて, しめる-しめて.
Take 5 ます-forms you already use (たべます, みます, ねます…), cover the answer and swap ます for て out loud.
In your notebook, split this lesson's vocabulary into 3 columns: る-verbs, う-verbs and irregulars. Mark かえる and はいる with ★.

grammar.title: う-verbs: the て-form table
grammar.explanation:
With う-verbs, the て-form depends on the **last syllable** of the dictionary form. There are five groups. This is the table to memorize:
• **う・つ・る → って**: かう → かって · まつ → まって · かえる → かえって
• **む・ぶ・ぬ → んで**: のむ → のんで · あそぶ → あそんで · しぬ → しんで
• **く → いて**: かく → かいて · きく → きいて
• **ぐ → いで**: いそぐ → いそいで · およぐ → およいで
• **す → して**: はなす → はなして · けす → けして
**Where the table comes from:** start from the ます-stem and let the て "slur" onto it, the way words wear down in fast speech: かき+て → かいて · いそぎ+て → いそいで · のみ+て → のんで · まち+て → まって · かえり+て → かえって · はなし+て → はなして (no change). This happened long ago; today Japanese speakers don't run the process in their heads — the slurred form is simply the word. So the table is not random, and after enough reading and listening you will recognize these forms at a glance.
**Trick 1: the song.** Repeat it in rhythm, like a chorus: "う つ る って · む ぶ ぬ んで · く いて · ぐ いで · す して". There are sung versions on YouTube (search "te-form song"); many people use the tune of "Oh My Darling, Clementine".
**Trick 2: where で appears.** Whenever the ending turns into **ん**, the て after it becomes voiced: ん + て → **んで** (む, ぶ, ぬ). And ぐ keeps its two little marks (゛): **いで**. Every other ending gives て.
**Trick 3: only one common verb ends in ぬ.** It is しぬ (to die). You'll hardly ever use it, but it completes the group.
• Going further (Sakubi): the plain past you'll learn in lesson 09-1 uses exactly the same sound changes, with た/だ in place of て/で: かって → かった, のんで → のんだ, かいて → かいた, いそいで → いそいだ. Learn this table well now and the past short forms come almost for free.
grammar.structure: う・つ・る → って · む・ぶ・ぬ → んで · く → いて · ぐ → いで · す → して

examples.jp: バスを まつ → バスを まって
examples.kana: バスを まつ → バスを まって
examples.romaji: basu o matsu → basu o matte
examples.en: to wait for the bus → て-form (つ → って)

examples.jp: おちゃを 飲む → おちゃを 飲んで
examples.kana: おちゃを のむ → おちゃを のんで
examples.romaji: ocha o nomu → ocha o nonde
examples.en: to drink tea → て-form (む → んで)

examples.jp: てがみを かく → てがみを かいて
examples.kana: てがみを かく → てがみを かいて
examples.romaji: tegami o kaku → tegami o kaite
examples.en: to write a letter → て-form (く → いて)

examples.jp: でんきを けす → でんきを けして
examples.kana: でんきを けす → でんきを けして
examples.romaji: denki o kesu → denki o keshite
examples.en: to turn off the light → て-form (す → して)

pitfalls: The small っ counts: まて ✗ → まって ✓ (ma-t-te, with a one-beat pause). Without it, まて becomes a different form: a blunt order, "wait!".
く and ぐ become いて and いで: かくて ✗ → かいて ✓ · いそいて ✗ → いそいで ✓ (ぐ keeps its two little marks). くて does exist, but it belongs to adjectives (lesson 07-2).
The る → って row is only for う-verbs, so check the group first: みる → みって ✗ → みて ✓ (みる is a る-verb), but かえる → かえって ✓ (a う-verb).
There are two きる: きる "to wear" is a る-verb (きて); きる "to cut" is a う-verb (きって). Same sound, different て-form.
howToStudy: Speaking: recite the table (う つ る って…) out loud 5 times. Then write it from memory in your notebook and check it.
Cover the answers and say the て-form of these verbs: かう, まつ, のむ, あそぶ, かく, いそぐ, はなす, かえる, やすむ, はいる. In your notebook, write down every mistake together with the verb's ending.
ヅオリンゴー → Practice L6: do one round of conjugation. After each mistake, say the verb's rule out loud (e.g. "む → んで").

grammar.title: Irregulars して / きて and the exception いって
grammar.gloss: the three that break the rule
grammar.explanation:
Three verbs don't follow the table. They are among the most common verbs, so it's worth memorizing them like vocabulary:
• **する → して** (to do). This applies to every verb with する: べんきょうする → べんきょうして · そうじする → そうじして · せんたくする → せんたくして.
• **くる → きて** (to come). The vowel changes to **き**, the same as in the ます-form (きます).
• **いく → いって** (to go). By the table, く would give いて (いいて), but いく is the **one everyday exception** among う-verbs and becomes いって, with っ.
• **Only する and くる are truly irregular.** いく is a normal う-verb everywhere else (いきます, いきません); only its て-form — and, later, its past いった — is special.
**Shortcut for the irregulars:** the て-form is the ます-form with て in place of ます. します → して, きます → きて. With う-verbs this shortcut doesn't work: いきます does not become いきて.
• A word you'll come across: もってくる ("to bring"). Literally it is もって ("holding", from もつ) + くる ("to come"). The て-form even shows up inside words.
• Going further (Sakubi): もってくる is one case of a pattern you'll use a lot — verb-て + a second verb that shapes the meaning of the first, often losing its own literal meaning. 〜ている (lesson 07-1) and 〜てあげる / 〜てもらう (lesson 16-1) are built this way.
grammar.structure: する → して · くる → きて · いく → いって (exception)

examples.jp: にほんごを べんきょうする → にほんごを べんきょうして
examples.kana: にほんごを べんきょうする → にほんごを べんきょうして
examples.romaji: nihongo o benkyō suru → nihongo o benkyō shite

examples.jp: うちに くる → うちに きて
examples.kana: うちに くる → うちに きて
examples.romaji: uchi ni kuru → uchi ni kite
examples.en: to come to my house → て-form

examples.jp: 大学に 行く → 大学に 行って
examples.kana: だいがくに いく → だいがくに いって
examples.romaji: daigaku ni iku → daigaku ni itte
examples.en: to go to college → て-form (the exception!)

pitfalls: いく → いいて ✗ → いって ✓. This is the exception that trips people up most: drill it until it comes out on its own.
くる → くって ✗ / くて ✗ → きて ✓. Think of the ます-form: き-ます → き-て.
する → すって ✗ → して ✓. In compounds, only する changes: べんきょうして ✓.
The "swap ます for て" shortcut only works for る-verbs and the irregulars: のみます → のみて ✗ (the right form is のんで).
howToStudy: Speaking: say these 10 times, switching fast: する-して, くる-きて, いく-いって.
Pick 3 of your own activities with する (べんきょう, そうじ, せんたく…) and say the て-form of each one out loud.
Speaking: record yourself saying every verb in the vocabulary list in the て-form. The goal is under 1 minute, without getting stuck. Keep the recording to compare later.

practice.what: Play normally and hunt for て-forms in the dialogues: words ending in …って, …んで, …いて, …いで or …して right after a piece of a verb. Write 3 of them in your notebook and use the table to work out each one's dictionary form, then check your guess in a dictionary (Yomitan or jisho.org show the dictionary form). Save the clearest line to ヅオリンゴー's Mining. If none show up yet, write down verbs in ます and make their て-form yourself.

Lesson 6 vocabulary in the SRS: first clear today's reviews (🌊 All), then learn the new verbs. Doing your reviews every day matters more than adding many new cards — if they pile up, add fewer new ones instead of skipping reviews. Then Practice L6: one round of conjugation, paying attention to the て-form.
Read the Sakubi section on the て form (linked in block 6) once, straight through. Aim to understand the idea, not to memorize it: the drills, the song and the game will do the memorizing.
Phone timer: 1 minute to say the て-form of 15 verbs from this lesson, in random order. Write down how many you got right and try to beat that score next session.

Tap 🔊 on each example and repeat along 3 times. Exaggerate the pause of っ (まって, いって) and the ん (のんで): in Japanese, each one takes a full beat. In natural speech the i of して is often whispered (it can sound like "shte"): copy what you hear. Still mixing up て/で or っ/つ when reading? Add 10 minutes of kana-flow or the Kana Trail.

culture.title: Lines and order (ならぶ)
culture.body: In Japan, lining up — **ならぶ** ("to line up") — is almost automatic. On train platforms there are usually marks on the floor showing where the doors will open, and people wait in line beside them, letting passengers get off first. A long line outside a restaurant is usually seen as a sign that the place is good, and many people join it on purpose. Cutting in line, or saving a spot for someone who hasn't arrived yet, is frowned upon. On escalators, people generally stand on one side only (usually the left in Tokyo and the right in Osaka), although many stations now ask people not to walk on them at all. And the て-form of ならぶ appears a lot on signs: **ならんで** ("lining up"), which follows the rule ぶ → んで.
culture.try: Say the て-form of ならぶ and まつ (ならんで, まって). Next time you're in a line, repeat ならんで、まって… under your breath and notice where the line starts and which way it moves.

checklist: I can recite the て-form table (う つ る って · む ぶ ぬ んで · く いて · ぐ いで · す して) without looking.
I can make the て-form of any る-verb (たべて, みて, あけて) without thinking.
I get the て-form of う-verbs right for all five endings, including いそいで and はなして.
I remember that かえる and はいる are う-verbs: かえって, はいって.
I don't get the three special ones wrong: して, きて, いって.
